title: RUN up high, a full-screen button and a natural voice
lede: RUN now sits high on the left, out of the walking thumb's way; a new button fills the screen wherever the browser allows it and explains the Home Screen route on iPhone; and the announcer speaks in a natural recorded voice that comes with the game, the same on every device.

sections.title: RUN, up out of the thumb's way
sections.html:
The thumb that walks rests low on the left, where the walking drag starts, and RUN sat in its path: on a phone on its side about two thirds of the way down the left edge, and on taller screens lower still. RUN now sits high on the left, out of that path:

  • A phone on its side (every screen up to 430 points tall): beside the small map and level with its middle, 54 points across. The left edge keeps clear of the notch's safe area, so on a phone with the notch on the left it moves in with the map.
  • Everything else (phones upright, iPads, computers): just under the small map, 256 points from the top, 60 points across. On a short phone held upright, such as the first iPhone SE (320 by 568), the map is a little smaller and RUN sits 228 points down, so it stays in the upper half there too.

It still toggles: one tap to run, one to walk, lit while running, and Shift on a keyboard. Apple's talk on touch controls for games puts the most used actions near the thumbs and less frequent ones towards the top of the screen (WWDC 2026, Make your game great with touch; WWDC Notes). RUN is pressed once to start running, not held, so it can sit up there, while the walking area keeps the lower left to itself.

Other buttons moved with it: the toasts on a phone on its side keep clear of RUN beside the map, the compass and goal line leave room for the new full-screen button at the top right, and on an upright phone the top buttons are 38 points across so five fit beside the health bar.

sections.title: A full-screen button
sections.html:
A new button, the first in the row at the top right during play and in the top right corner of the title screen, puts the game in full screen through the browser's Fullscreen API. While the game fills the screen the four corners point inwards and the button reads Leave full screen; a tap leaves, and so does Esc on a keyboard. Going in or out does not pause the game.

How it works

  • The request goes to the whole page (document.documentElement.requestFullscreen({ navigationUI: 'hide' })), so the HUD, the small map and every menu come along. navigationUI: 'hide' asks the browser to give the whole screen to the game instead of keeping its own controls on view (MDN, requestFullscreen).
  • Browsers allow the request only during a tap or a click (MDN, the Fullscreen standard). The button acts on the touch itself, the same way as the other buttons at the top since the iPhone fix in commit 524a864, and a touch counts as such a tap.
  • Older Safari on iPad and Mac knows only the webkit names, which the button falls back to.
  • The icon and label follow what the browser actually did, read back after every request, on the browser's change event and on the resize that comes with it, so leaving with Esc or a swipe also updates the button.
  • If the browser refuses, a short note says so. If the browser takes the request and does nothing for one and a half seconds, which an iPhone can do (bugnet), the note says what works there instead.

On iPhone

Safari on iPhone lets only videos fill the screen; the Fullscreen API on other parts of a page is limited to iPad (Can I use, which lists iPhone and iPad Safari 12 to 26.3 as partial, iPad only; Apple Developer Forums; Apple Developer Forums, iOS 17). Apple has an iPhone version behind a Safari feature flag, which ordinary users do not turn on (WebKit bug 266232). The game does not look for the word iPhone: it asks the browser whether full screen is available. So the day Safari on iPhone allows it, the button works there with no change.

Until then, on an iPhone the button explains the way that does work: add the game to the Home Screen and start it from its icon. The game's web app manifest asks for "display": "fullscreen" and its page carries apple-mobile-web-app-capable, so from the Home Screen it opens without Safari's address bar and buttons (MDN, display; Apple, Configuring Web Applications), with the page drawn under the status bar (black-translucent). Since iOS 26 every site added to the Home Screen opens this way by default, with an Open as Web App switch that is on (heise), and Share has moved into the ··· menu beside the address bar (iThinkDiff); the note and the README say so. Started from the Home Screen, or in the iOS app, the game already fills the screen and the button is hidden.

Inside the Claude app or the artifact page on an iPhone the game runs inside another page, and an iPhone does not let anything inside another page fill the screen. There the note says so: the game has to be on its own page (for example npm run serve on your Wi-Fi network, as the README describes) before it can go on the Home Screen. On a computer the artifact page allows full screen from a click.

sections.title: The announcer's own voice
sections.html:
The last two rounds made the announcer pick the most natural voice the phone has and explain how to download a better one. That still leaves the phone's own voices, and an iPhone ships only compact ones, which sound flat. So the voice now comes with the game: every line the announcer says, and every name it says after one, was spoken ahead of time by Kokoro-82M, an openly licensed neural speech model (Apache License 2.0), and ships inside the game as small sound files. It sounds the same on every phone, tablet and computer, with nothing to download or set up.

  • What is recorded: 145 clips, 146 seconds in all. That is all 55 announcer lines ("Fish on!", "It threw the hook!", "Spooled! It took all your line!"), the 31 fish and 9 legends, the telescope's 18 targets, the meteorites, where a fireball came down, the space weather warnings, the bears, the finds and the speed records.
  • How it is packed: each clip is trimmed, set to the same loudness and stored as a 24 kHz mono MP3 at 32 kbps, 607 KB in all, inside the game's single file (which grows from 2,007 to 2,823 KB). A clip is decoded the first time it is needed, and the eleven most heard lines are decoded in the background a moment after the game starts (not during the tap that starts it), so the first "Fish on!" is not late.
  • How it plays: through the game's own sound, so it follows the volume setting, and the wind, water and music dip by 5 dB while it talks. A new line cuts off the last one. A line and a name play one after the other ("New species!" then "Northern pike!"). A personal best says the fish, and the weight stays on the banner. A name with no recording is shown and not said.
  • Settings, Voice starts on Game voice; each tap plays a sample and moves on to the device's own natural voices (still never the novelty ones), then back. Anyone who picked a device voice in an earlier version is moved to the game's voice once, and can pick theirs again. The note about downloading Enhanced voices now appears only if a device voice is picked.
  • Pronunciation: the speech model read every name as written except four, which are respelled for it: Albireo, Mizar and Alcor, Bode's Galaxy and Kokanee. Numbers are spelled out ("two hundred kilometres an hour").

The tools that make the clips are in the repository (tools/voice), so a new line or fish can be recorded the same way; the README has the steps. A line without a recording is still said, in the device's voice.

Every clip: speech level -22.0 to -20.0 dB, peaks no higher than -1.5 dB, 0.58 to 2.24 seconds long (1.01 on average).

sections.title: What the review found, and what was fixed
sections.html:
A separate reviewer read this round's code without running it: the layout rules, the full-screen button, the voice player and the settings change. It confirmed five defects and raised two more points. All seven were fixed, and the checks were extended to cover them.

#FoundWhat went wrongFixed, and checked by
1The compass and goal squeezed on screens 600 to 709 wide and taller than 430Room for a fifth top button left a 7-inch tablet held upright (600 by 960) with a compass 40 points wide and a goal of two letters. The layout check jumped from 507 to 820 wide and missed it.Those screens now use the narrow layout, with the compass and goal under the top row. The layout check now also measures 320, 600, 673 and 744 wide.
2Room kept for a hidden buttonStarted from the Home Screen or in the iOS app, the full-screen button is hidden, but the compass and goal still left room for it: 222 points instead of 318 on a notched iPhone on its side.The room for the top row is now a variable that drops back when the button is hidden. Checked in the layout check (the Home Screen case) and the Home Screen check.
3A voice line could play after it was stoppedA line still being decoded when the game paused, went back to the title or the voice was turned off started a moment later anyway, over the pause menu or the title.Stopping now also cancels a line in decoding, and a replaced line that fails to decode no longer falls back to the device voice. The voice check stops a line mid-decode and finds nothing playing and the sound of the place back at full.
4Wrong or doubled full-screen notesA browser that refused showed its refusal and then, 1.5 seconds later, a second note saying the browser cannot do full screen at all. Going in and out within 1.5 seconds did the same. Each tap on an iPhone added another copy of the note.A refusal or any change of state cancels the waiting check, and a note already showing is not repeated. The iPhone check taps twice and counts one note, then tries a refusing browser and finds only the refusal.
5Top buttons touching the health bar under 360 wideOn the first iPhone SE upright, or in Slide Over on an iPad, five buttons reached the health bar, and the money once it passed $1,000.Smaller buttons, health bar and money under 360 wide. Measured at 320 by 568 with $1,500.
6The title-screen note cut off on a short screenThe reviewer suspected it and a check confirmed it: in Safari on an iPhone on its side, with the browser's bars, the screen is about 330 tall, and the note ran past the bottom (to 351 of 330).The note now shows in a small panel right under the full-screen button: 62 to 165 of 330.
7A click on the button also captured the mouseOn a computer, any click in the game also captures the mouse for looking round, so going full screen from the button hid the pointer too.A click on the full-screen button now stays with the button. The computer check counts no capture after the button and one after a click on the view.

Checked and found sound: the full-screen request runs inside the tap itself, which browsers require; the button follows the real state through the browser's events; RUN clears the chips, the toasts, the hints and the driving controls in every mode; the voice's memory is bounded and the sound of the place never stays dipped; every line and name in the code has a recording; and the settings change moves an old device voice to the game's voice only once.

sections.title: What this report cannot show
sections.html:
• No real iPhone or iPad was used. The phone checks run in Chromium set up like an iPhone 15: its screen sizes, touch, Safari's user agent and, for the full-screen checks, Safari on iPhone's missing Fullscreen API (taken out of the page before it loads). Safari itself may differ, for example in how it turns the request down; the button handles a refusal, a missing API and a request ignored without a word, and each of those was imitated.
  • Full screen in the test browser has no real screen. Headless Chromium enters and leaves full screen, and the game's button follows, but the window stays 960 by 540, and the browser applies the change only when it draws its next frame. The pictures show the button's state, not what a monitor looks like in full screen.
  • The artifact page was not tested on a computer or a phone; the claims about it come from how the browser treats a page inside another page.
  • Whether RUN is now out of the way for your hand is a matter of how you hold the phone. The checks prove where it is and that nothing overlaps it, at fourteen screen sizes, not how it feels.
  • Frame times come from a software renderer on the processor, many times slower than a phone's graphics chip. They compare this build with the last one on the same machine; they do not predict a phone's frame rate.
  • The voice. How natural a voice sounds cannot be measured by a test, and nobody listened to it on a phone here. The checks prove that every recording decodes and plays, in the right order, through the game's sound. The device voices in Settings were checked against a typed-in list imitating an iPhone's English voices; the real list depends on the phone, its language and what has been downloaded.
  • The silent switch. Like every other sound in the game, the new voice plays through the browser's Web Audio, which Safari on iPhone mutes while the ring/silent switch is on silent (Audjust, WebKit bug 237322). The device voices used before may not have followed the switch, so with the phone on silent the announcer is now as quiet as the rest of the game.
  • Sources were read through web search. curl is blocked for every host in this environment, so the pages listed below were found and summarised by search, not downloaded in full. To allow hosts: the cloud environment menu in the session's title bar, then Edit, then Network access (a broader level, or Custom with the hosts added under Allowed domains); the steps are at https://code.claude.com/docs/en/cloud-environments#network-access.

sections.title: What would change this conclusion
sections.html:
The conclusion: RUN is out of the walking thumb's way at every screen size checked, the full-screen button works wherever the browser allows full screen and explains the Home Screen route where it does not (Safari on iPhone), the announcer now speaks in a natural recorded voice on every device, and nothing from the earlier rounds broke. It would change if:

  • The new voice still does not sound right to you. The speech model has other voices, among them men's and British ones; the tool in the repository records the whole set again with another in about seven minutes, and the game needs no other change.
  • You still hit RUN by accident on a real phone, for example because your thumb starts the walk high on the left. Then RUN should need a deliberate press, such as a short hold, or move to the right-hand side above the tool button.
  • Safari on a real iPhone answers the request in a way none of the imitations covers, such as going part way into full screen. The iPhone version behind Safari's feature flag has shown the page behind leaking through at the top and white bars in landscape (WebKit bug 266232). If that reached ordinary iPhones, the button should stay with the Home Screen note on iPhone instead of asking.
  • Apple turns the Fullscreen API on for iPhone by default. Then the button simply starts working there, because it asks the browser rather than looking for an iPhone, and the note stops showing.
  • A Home Screen launch does not fill the screen on your iPhone, for example with Open as Web App switched off on iOS 26 (heise). Then the note should mention the switch.
  • A real phone shows a steady cost from this round. In the test browser the two builds are equal at an iPhone's size, and this one is about 0.7 ms a frame slower at the smallest size, most likely from the voice recordings held in the script's memory (keeping them as page text did not clearly help). If a phone shows it too, the next step is to measure there with and without the recordings. A voice clip's first use is not a likely stall: turning its few kilobytes of text into bytes takes well under a millisecond, and the browser decodes the sound away from the thread that draws.
